newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine traders disagree over soy frost damage.
newsitem.headline: Argentine traders disagree over soy frost damage.

text.p: Argentine traders disagreed Monday over whether weekend frosts which hit parts of the soybean crop caused much damage.
"We hear it's nothing serious," one trader told Reuters, "There were a couple of very slight frosts, with no major damage caused."

The trader, who said he was sticking to his forecast of a 12.5-million-tonne harvest, said he was not at all concerned about the frosts which hit southern Santa Fe near Rosario and northern and western parts of Buenos Aires Friday and Saturday nights. He said that the frosts did not last long and that the temperature did not fall much below freezing.
Two other export traders consulted by Reuters agreed that there had been little damage.

"For the moment, we have the impression that there was no significant damage," one said, "But the thing is we are in a very sensitive stage, and there is a possibility we might get some more frosts this coming weekend due to a cold front on the way."

He said the west of Buenos Aires was the zone hardest hit by the frosts but added he was holding his forecast for output steady at 12.2 million tonnes. "The most damage so far has been from the dry weather earlier on," he said.
Another trader said he thought the frosts had caused damage.

"It's hard at this time to estimate how much damage was casued," he said, "But undoubtedly at this stage in the season a frost inhibits pod filling. We won't know by how much until after the harvest."
Second crop beans, which make up about 40 percent of Argentina's planting this season, are still in the pod-filling phase.
The trader was pessimistic about the soybean crop.
"Before the frost I thought it would be difficult to make 12 million tonnes," he said, "Now I'm even more doubtful. I rule out 12.5 million tonnes totally."

The Argentine government in mid-March reduced its soybean output forecast to 13.5 million tonnes from 13.9 million tonnes after dry weather. Most in the industry said at the time it should have cut its estimate to between 12.5 million and 13 million tonnes.
